prompt.context: Our client sells software that runs on hospital operating systems across the nation. The software is used for administrative tasks, such as back-office operations and clinical record-keeping. The company used to be a market leader, but its share has steadily been declining. Specifically, sales have dropped. Our client has engaged our consulting firm to find out why sales have dropped and to provide recommendations that will address this issue.
prompt.question: First, please size the US market for this hospital administrative software. Then, identify why sales have been declining and provide recommendations to address the issue.

clarifying_info.q: What is the replacement rate for the software?
clarifying_info.a: Hospitals replace their software every 10 years.

clarifying_info.q: How much is a software sale worth and how is payment structured?
clarifying_info.a: Each software sale is worth $9M, but because it takes 3 years to install, the company receives the money in three installments of $3M per year.

clarifying_info.q: How many software products does each hospital need?
clarifying_info.a: Only one software product is needed per hospital.

clarifying_info.q: What is the market growth rate?
How does our client's installation time compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Competition can install their products within 2 years; our client sometimes takes up to 4 years.

clarifying_info.q: What does the sales force say about selling the product?
clarifying_info.a: The sales force says the product is hard to sell to hospitals. Installments can be delayed and can take sometimes up to 4 years to complete installation.

clarifying_info.q: What happens when installations are delayed?
clarifying_info.a: When installations are delayed, software patches have to be developed to make the software function properly in the meantime, which is costly in terms of programming and training costs.

clarifying_info.q: What do customers say about the product?
clarifying_info.a: Customers prefer simple products that are easy to use and navigate. They feel the client's product has more features than needed, making it complex and lengthening installation time.

clarifying_info.q: How does the R&D unit operate?
clarifying_info.a: The R&D unit often adds features to the product without any market research first.

exhibits.shows: Supporting exhibit from the case on PDF page 73

framework: External environment: market growth rate, industry changes, new legislation or technology, competitor products, customer preferences
Internal analysis: product fit vs. customer standards, pricing vs. competitors, R&D capabilities and process, sales force compensation and effectiveness, sales and marketing performance

questions.prompt: Size the US market for hospital administrative software (annual revenue opportunity).
questions.guidance: Candidate should build up from population to hospitals, apply replacement rate to get annual unit demand, then multiply by price per unit. Strong answer uses a logical anchor (e.g., 1 hospital per 50,000 people) and clearly states assumptions.

math.setup: Estimate number of US hospitals from population, apply 10-year replacement cycle to get annual demand, multiply by $9M unit price.
steps: Annual replacements: 6,000 hospitals / 10-year cycle = 600 units per year
Annual market revenue: 600 units x $9M = $5.4B per year

questions.prompt: Why have sales been declining? What are the key root causes?
questions.guidance: Strong candidates examine both external and internal factors. External: market is growing 15% so the problem is not market contraction but share loss; competitors install faster (2 years vs. up to 4 years). Internal: product is overly complex with unnecessary features, making it hard to sell and slow to install; delayed installs require costly patches; R&D adds features without market research, compounding complexity.

brainstorming.prompt: What are the factors making the client's product difficult to sell and implement?

categories.name: Product complexity
ideas: Too many features beyond customer needs
Harder to train hospital staff on complex system

categories.name: Implementation / operations
ideas: Installation takes up to 4 years vs. 2 years for competitors
Delayed installations require costly software patches
Patch development increases programming and training costs

categories.name: R&D process
ideas: R&D adds features without market research
No structured policy for evaluating new feature additions
Feature bloat driven internally, not by customer demand

categories.name: Sales force
ideas: Product is hard to sell given complexity
Sales force may lack effective messaging or support
Customer objections around complexity and long implementation timeline

categories.name: Customer preferences
ideas: Customers feel the product has more features than needed
Preference for shorter, predictable implementation timelines

recommendation: Simplify the product by reducing unnecessary features to make it easier to use, easier to sell, and faster to implement — targeting installation time on par with competitors (2 years).
Establish R&D control policies that require market research and customer validation before any new features are added to the product roadmap.
risks: Simplifying the product may require significant re-engineering investment and a transition period.
Existing customers on the current complex platform may require continued patch support during any transition.
Competitors may continue to innovate and gain share during the simplification effort.
next_steps: Conduct customer research to identify which features are truly valued vs. which add unnecessary complexity.
Benchmark competitor products to define a simplified feature set that meets market needs.
Design a phased product simplification roadmap with clear milestones for reducing installation time.
Implement R&D governance: require market research sign-off before any new feature enters development.
